subtype: My view is the only view [Actor]
passage:
Note for Vikas's parents, Tuesday, rainy afternoon.
Vikas played hiding today by pressing both palms over his eyes in the middle of the rug. "Vikas gone!" he shouted, his feet sticking out plainly. His big sister Vasudha giggled, "I can see you, silly!" He kept his hands there, sure he had vanished. Later he held his picture book up facing himself and told Vasudha, "Look, elephant!" I turned the book round for her and said, "Now Didi can see it too." He looked very surprised. 🙂

qa.q: What did Vikas do with his picture book?
qa.a: He held it up facing himself and told Vasudha to look at the elephant.

qa.q: Why did Vikas keep his hands over his eyes even after Vasudha said she could see him?
qa.a: He felt sure and delighted that he had vanished 😊; at his age, if he cannot see others he believes they cannot see him either.

qa.q: How could the caregiver keep helping Vikas notice that others see differently?
qa.a: Keep playing gently, turning pictures round and saying things like "Now Didi sees it", without teasing, so he slowly learns that others look from a different place.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see Vikas's hiding game?
qa.a: She finds it funny, because she can clearly see his feet and body; she already knows that covering your own eyes does not hide you.

grounding: A toddler covers his own eyes to hide and shows a picture facing himself, not yet grasping that others see things differently.

passage: The week before Christmas, the preschool corridor smelled of glue and cotton-wool snow. When Sumit came to collect his son, Akash ran up shouting, "It fell down and she cried and then the big one came!" Sumit crouched. "What fell? Who cried?" Akash frowned as if his father were being slow. "The star, Papa! You know!" He pointed at a bare hook near the ceiling. Then he held out his half-eaten slice of plum cake. "You want this, na? You love plum cake." Sumit, who did not much like plum cake, took a small bite anyway.

qa.q: What did Akash point to when he talked about the star?
qa.a: He pointed at a bare hook near the ceiling.

qa.q: Why did Akash frown when his father asked "What fell?"
qa.a: He felt puzzled and a little impatient, because he assumed Papa already knew what had happened at school, as if his own memory were shared.

qa.q: What small step would help Sumit get the full story?
qa.a: Ask one simple question at a time, such as "Where were you when the star fell?", and repeat the pieces back so Akash learns to fill in what Papa did not see.

qa.q: What is it like for Sumit when Akash tells the story this way?
qa.a: He is confused and has to guess, but he stays patient and even eats cake he does not like to keep Akash happy.

grounding: A preschooler gives a puzzling half-story as if his father saw it too, and assumes his father shares his love of plum cake.

passage: It was kite week before Sankranti at the community centre crèche, and paper diamonds hung from every window. Ganga yanked the pink kite out of little Rashi's hands. Rashi howled. Farida, the teacher, knelt beside Ganga with her box of face cards. "Which face is Rashi making?" Ganga pointed at the crying card. "Sad." "Why sad?" Ganga thought. "Kite gone." Farida said, "From where Rashi stands, the kite just disappeared." She picked up two sock puppets. "This one is Ganga, this one is Rashi. Show me." Ganga made her puppet grab, then stopped. "Rashi puppet cries," she said quietly, and carried the real kite back.

qa.q: What did Farida use to help Ganga?
qa.a: She used a box of face cards and two sock puppets.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she made her puppet stop grabbing?
qa.a: She seemed sorry and a little ashamed, because acting out the grab let her feel what losing the kite was like for Rashi.

qa.q: Which choice by Farida worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Ganga to name Rashi's face and replay it with puppets worked, because Ganga found the other child's feeling herself instead of just being scolded.

qa.q: How might Rashi see the moment Ganga brings the kite back?
qa.a: Rashi would likely feel relieved and surprised, and may trust Ganga more when they play together next time.

grounding: A caregiver uses picture cards, pretend play and her own words about another child's view to help a preschooler take that child's perspective.

passage: On the first frosty morning of winter football camp, Harsha and Francis were picking positions. Francis wanted to be goalkeeper. Harsha hated standing in goal and used to think everyone did. "Okay, you like the gloves, I get it," Harsha said, handing them over. By the second half, though, Harsha's side was losing three–nil and the coach moved Harsha back to defence. "Francis, swap with me. You'd rather be out here, obviously!" Francis shook his head. "I told you, I like goal." Harsha kicked the white grass. "Nobody likes standing in goal when we're losing." Francis just pulled the gloves tighter and faced the pitch.

qa.q: Which position did Francis want to play?
qa.a: Francis wanted to be goalkeeper.

qa.q: Why did Harsha insist that Francis would rather swap?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and embarrassed about losing, and that strong feeling pushed him back into assuming Francis must want what he wanted.

qa.q: What could Harsha try next time he is upset during a match?
qa.a: Take a breath and ask "Do you still want goal?" instead of deciding for Francis; his own feelings can be real without being Francis's too.

qa.q: How does Francis feel when Harsha tells him what he would rather do?
qa.a: He likely feels unheard and a bit annoyed, since he had already said he likes goal; pulling the gloves tighter shows he is holding his ground.

grounding: An older child accepts that a friend wants something different, but slips back into assuming his own wants when losing makes his feelings strong.

passage:
Camp log, monsoon nature camp, days one to four.
Day one: Omkar kept his hood up at every meal. When I asked, he said, "Nobody here gets what it's like to switch schools three times. And everyone stared when I slipped on the path." Nobody had; most were busy scraping mud off their own shoes.
Day three: during the leech check, Chandrika mentioned she had moved cities twice. Omkar looked at her as if she had spoken a secret language. They talked until the lamps went off.
Day four: he slipped again and laughed, and so did two others. I paired him with Chandrika for the river walk and told him that half this group arrived as newcomers. "Seriously? Half?" he said.
Next: I will remind everyone about the group chat so they keep in touch after camp.

qa.q: What did Chandrika mention during the leech check?
qa.a: She mentioned that she had moved cities twice.

qa.q: Why did Omkar believe everyone stared when he slipped?
qa.a: He felt self-conscious and alone, so his own embarrassment seemed like the centre of everyone's attention, even though most were busy with their own muddy shoes.

qa.q: What did the camp leader do that helped, and what could come next?
qa.a: Pairing Omkar with Chandrika and telling him many were newcomers widened his view; keeping the group in touch after camp can help that last.

qa.q: How is Chandrika affected when Omkar finds out she shares his experience?
qa.a: She likely feels connected too, since they talked until the lamps went off; her small remark helped someone else feel less alone.

grounding: A teenager feels nobody shares his experience and that all eyes are on him, and the feeling softens as he meets others with similar stories.

passage: Nitin came home from tuition, dropped his bag in the doorway of the Pune flat and announced, "My life is literally over. I wore the wrong shoes to the farewell and everyone will remember it forever." Sudha, his mother, was chopping onions and felt the old urge to say, "Nobody cares about your shoes." Then she remembered crying over a bad haircut at his age. Instead she said, "That sounds awful to walk in with." Nitin sat down and talked for twenty minutes. A week later, over tea, Sudha asked what his friend Arvind had worn. Nitin paused. "Actually, Arvind's trousers were torn. No one said anything." He looked at her, half embarrassed, half amused. Sudha only smiled and passed the biscuits.

qa.q: What did Nitin say had gone wrong at the farewell?
qa.a: He said he wore the wrong shoes to the farewell.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she held back "Nobody cares about your shoes"?
qa.a: She felt tempted and a little impatient, but remembering her own teenage upset made her sympathetic, so she chose to listen instead.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Listening first and asking about Arvind a week later worked, because Nitin felt taken seriously and then noticed by himself that others have awkward moments too.

qa.q: How does Nitin see the shoe problem once Sudha has listened?
qa.a: At first it feels huge and permanent to him; a week later he sees that Arvind's torn trousers went unnoticed and feels half embarrassed about his worry.

grounding: A parent treats her teenager's self-focus as a normal stage, listens without dismissing it, and later gently widens his view.

passage: Snow pressed against the windows of the Toronto apartment on the last day of winter break. Mei, the babysitter, heard a clink from the kitchen. Jana stood by the table, hands behind her back. Cocoa spread in a brown puddle under the snowman mug, and a thin crack ran down its side. "Did something spill?" Mei asked. "No," Jana said quickly. "It was always like that." "The crack too?" "There's no crack." Jana stared at the ceiling, cheeks pink. Mei grabbed a cloth. "Accidents happen. Let's wipe it together." Jana's shoulders dropped a little, but she still whispered, "I didn't do it."

qa.q: Which mug had the crack?
qa.a: The snowman mug, with cocoa spreading under it.

qa.q: Why did Jana say there was no crack?
qa.a: She was scared of being in trouble 😰, so saying it never happened felt safer, as if the crack might disappear if she did not admit it.

qa.q: What could Mei try to make telling the truth easier for Jana?
qa.a: Keep the tone calm, name the fact simply, and thank Jana for helping clean up, so being honest feels safe next time.

qa.q: What would change if Mei had shouted instead?
qa.a: Jana would probably feel even more frightened and hold on harder to "I didn't do it".

grounding: A young child denies a spill and a cracked cup because fear of trouble is stronger than the wish to be accurate.

passage:
Before: Three days before Diwali, Tejas overheard Papa telling Chandrika, his mother, that the factory had let him go. When Aai sat Tejas down to explain, he said, "It's fine, Aai. Papa will get another one," and went back to stringing lights on the balcony.
During: On Diwali night he did not ask why there were fewer sweets. He snapped at his little cousin over a sparkler and lay awake long after the crackers stopped.
After: A week later, Chandrika found him awake again at midnight. "Is Papa sad?" he finally whispered. She sat on his bed and told him the plain truth: things were tight for now, but the grown-ups had a plan. Tejas fell asleep before she left the room.

qa.q: When did Tejas first hear about Papa's job?
qa.a: Three days before Diwali, when he overheard Papa telling Chandrika that the factory had let him go.

qa.q: Why did Tejas keep saying "It's fine"?
qa.a: He was frightened for Papa and the family 😔, and not knowing felt safer than facing it, though the worry leaked out as snapping and lying awake.

qa.q: How could a parent support a child like Tejas?
qa.a: Give simple, honest information without forcing talk, notice signs such as poor sleep and a short temper, and check in gently at calm moments.

qa.q: What was it like for Tejas's little cousin on Diwali night?
qa.a: The cousin was probably hurt and confused at being snapped at over a sparkler, not knowing the temper came from worry at home.

grounding: A child whose father lost a job insists all is fine and stops asking, while the worry shows in poor sleep and a short temper.

subtype: Facing a bad result in small doses [Response]
passage: When the chemistry marks came out in March, I told everyone I had done "fine". I even told myself the paper must have been marked wrong. For two weeks I did not open the answer sheet; it lived folded inside my geometry box. Then my cousin Madhuri asked about it at dinner, and something in me stopped pretending. Afterwards I showed her the sheet on the terrace. "Thirty-one out of eighty," I said out loud. Saying the number hurt, but less than hiding it had. Madhuri did not lecture. She just asked, "Okay, Gautam. Which chapters?" We circled three together. That night I wrote a weekly revision list and stuck it above my desk.

qa.q: Where did Gautam keep the answer sheet for two weeks?
qa.a: It lived folded inside the geometry box.

qa.q: Why did Gautam avoid opening the answer sheet?
qa.a: Gautam felt ashamed and afraid of the real number, and not looking softened the shock for a while.

qa.q: What helped Gautam move from hiding the result to acting on it?
qa.a: Saying the mark aloud to one trusted cousin, then circling three chapters together and writing a weekly list 🙏; small steps made the result manageable.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have felt when Gautam finally said the number?
qa.a: She was probably relieved that Gautam trusted her, and chose to stay calm and practical instead of lecturing.

grounding: A teenager who pretended a poor mark was fine says it aloud to a trusted cousin first, and then makes a plan.

passage:
Hostel warden's log, Block C, the week the winter fog set in.
Monday: Madhav came to my desk worried about his roommate. Harsha had three unopened letters from the accounts office and had failed two internal tests. When I asked Harsha, he laughed. "It'll sort itself out. First-term results are always weird."
Wednesday: The counsellor told me Harsha had not answered her two emails. At breakfast I saw him scroll straight past them.
Friday: The accounts office pinned the final date for fees on the notice board: next Tuesday. Harsha stood reading it for a long time, then knocked on my door, pale. I walked him to the counsellor's room that afternoon and asked someone from accounts to join. Madhav waited outside with two cups of tea.

qa.q: What did the accounts office pin on the notice board?
qa.a: The final date for fees: next Tuesday.

qa.q: Why did Harsha laugh and say it would sort itself out?
qa.a: He felt dread about the fees and marks, and not looking kept that fear at a distance, so ignoring the letters felt easier than opening them.

qa.q: What could have helped Harsha sooner?
qa.a: Opening one letter with Madhav or the warden early and replying to the counsellor would have let him get help before the deadline forced it.

qa.q: How is Madhav affected by Harsha's avoidance?
qa.a: Madhav is worried enough to go to the warden, yet stays loyal, waiting outside with tea when Harsha finally faces it.

grounding: A student ignores falling marks, unopened fee letters and the counsellor's messages until a deadline forces him to act.
